explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. God says to Ezekiel, "Then declare to them their abominations." Ezekiel is the one who has to speak it out loud. I think that's a heavy job, and it shows how seriously God takes what comes next.
Not this time, friend. The text says the opposite. God tells Ezekiel, "Then declare to them their abominations." He isn't asked to stay quiet or soften it. Ezekiel is told to say it plainly.

That's it. God says, "They have committed adultery with their idols." He uses the picture of a faithful marriage and says they gave themselves to something else. Idols are the other love in this picture.

Close to something a person might guess, but servants never show up in this verse. God says, "They have committed adultery with their idols." The unfaithfulness is about what they worshiped, not who worked for them.
Rivals would make it a story about neighbors competing, and that's not what's on the page. God says, "They have committed adultery with their idols." The other love in this picture is idols.

That's the opposite of what the text says. On the very day they slaughtered their children for their idols, "they entered My sanctuary to profane it." Then God adds, "Yes, they did this inside My house." They didn't stay away at all.

Right. The sisters didn't stay away. The text says that on the very day, "they entered My sanctuary to profane it." God says it happened "inside My house." I think this is one of the hardest lines in the whole passage.

explanations.answer: They bathe and paint their eyes
explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. God says, "you bathed for them, painted your eyes, and adorned yourself with jewelry." The sisters get ready for the men who came from afar, the way you'd get ready for company. Except this company wasn't God.
Bowing doesn't show up in this verse. God says the sisters "bathed for them, painted your eyes, and adorned yourself with jewelry." The picture is of getting themselves ready, not bowing down.
No gold gifts are handed over in this verse. The jewelry goes on the sisters themselves. God says they "bathed for them, painted your eyes, and adorned yourself with jewelry."

That's the one. God says the sisters sat on a couch with a table spread before it, "on which you had set My incense and My oil." Notice the words "My" in there. These were God's things, and they ended up on the wrong table.
Gold and silver are nowhere on this table. God says what was set on it was "My incense and My oil." Those are the things He calls His own in this verse.
A table does sound like bread and wine, I'll give you that. But the verse says something else. What's on the table is "My incense and My oil."

explanations.answer: She's been unfaithful a long time
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. "Grown old in adulteries" tells you the unfaithfulness isn't new. It's been going on for a long time. In this picture, she didn't wander off yesterday.

explanations.answer: She's too old to be judged now
explanations.explanation: Age isn't a shield here. The phrase is "grown old in adulteries," so the years are about how long she's been unfaithful. Later God says the sisters will be sentenced (Ezekiel 23:45). Getting older didn't get her out of it.
It's the other way around, friend. "Grown old in adulteries" points to a long stretch of unfaithfulness, not a fresh start. Someone who only just started wouldn't be described that way.

That's right. God says, "But righteous men will sentence them to the punishment of those who commit adultery and bloodshed…" The ones who sentence them are described as righteous. The sisters are charged with adultery and with blood on their hands.
Money isn't the point here. The word God uses for the men is "righteous." They aren't described by how much they own, but by what they are.
Age isn't mentioned for these men. The verse says, "But righteous men will sentence them…" What marks them is that they're righteous, not how young they are.

Yes. The mob will "…and burn down their houses." It's a heavy verse, and it comes right after the stoning and the swords. I think this is one of the places in the passage where it's right to go quiet for a second.
Nobody's moving in. The verse says the mob will "…and burn down their houses." The houses don't get taken over, they get destroyed. It's a heavy picture of the judgment.
Nobody is watching over the houses in this verse. The mob will "…and burn down their houses." It's a hard line, and I won't make it sound softer than it is.

True, baker. God says, "So I will put an end to indecency in the land…" He isn't leaving it. He says what He will do. The same verse says all the women will be admonished not to imitate the sisters' behavior.
The text says the opposite. God says, "So I will put an end to indecency in the land…" He says He will do it. It isn't left for someone else to sort out.

explanations.answer: That He is the Lord GOD
explanations.explanation: You nailed it. God ends with, "Then you will know that I am the Lord GOD." The whole passage closes on who He is. And that's the last passage in this group, so there's your ending.

The idols come out of this passage looking like the thing the sisters gave themselves to, not like something strong. The verse says, "Then you will know that I am the Lord GOD." What the sisters come to know is who God is.
Egypt isn't in this verse at all. Nobody is coming to rescue the sisters here. God says, "Then you will know that I am the Lord GOD."
